# Find a Park

A Phase 1 scaffold for a New York City-area park finder using the 12 supplied sample records.

## Run

From the repository root, using Node.js 24 and npm:

```powershell
npm install
npm run dev
```

Open the local URL printed by Vite.

## What works

The app loads and normalizes the sample. Three labeled placeholder regions show the planned layout. The list and details share the left pane, with the map on the right. The regions stack on a narrow screen.

## Left out

Resident-facing park selection, markers, tiles, and detail content are future work. Search, filters, geolocation, accounts, a backend, and deployment are outside this phase.

## Decisions

- Both JSON files are unchanged copies of the supplied sample. The app imports `src/data/parks.sample.json`. The brief names `assets/parks.sample.json`.
- Normalization requires a nonblank ID and name, trims text, and produces empty arrays for absent amenities and images. Invalid or incomplete coordinate pairs are discarded together. The park and any usable address are retained.
- `App` owns the selected ID. Map and list receive the same collection, selected ID, and selection callback. Details receives the matching park and a close callback. Each feature can be developed in its component folder.
- Brian has two open UX decisions for the details feature: whether to omit missing fields or label them â€œNot providedâ€, and what mobile Close/Back should return to after a list or marker selection.

## Known issues

The sample image URLs are placeholders. The details feature will need to handle a failed image load as well as an empty image array. The map feature will need to handle unavailable tiles while keeping the list and details usable.

## How it was checked

- `npm run build`, `npm test`, `npm run typecheck`, and `npm run lint` passed with Node.js 24.20.0 and npm 11.19.0.
- All 18 tests passed. They cover the sample's missing values, string cleanup, invalid and boundary coordinates, and rendering the three named regions with the full collection.
- SHA-256 hashes matched for the supplied JSON and both repository copies.
- A headless Chrome check of the production build measured the panes side by side at 1280 CSS pixels and stacked at 375, with no horizontal overflow at either width.

## Time spent

Approximately 3 minutes of elapsed scaffold and verification time in this session. This excludes prior planning and subsequent feature work.

## Next steps

1. **feature/map** â€” Use React Leaflet and OpenStreetMap tiles. Fit bounds to valid markers, connect marker selection to details, distinguish the selected marker, and handle tile failure. The map should work without a location prompt.
2. **feature/list** â€” Render a count and a name-sorted semantic list of buttons. Support keyboard selection, visible focus, and an accessible current-park indication.
3. **feature/details** â€” Show supplied fields, humanize amenity slugs, preserve hours as written, and handle missing fields and failed images. Focus the heading on selection and support mobile Close/Back.
4. After integration, exercise both selection paths on a phone and desktop, including keyboard-only use, focus movement, image failure, and tile failure.

 Find a Park Take Home
 Candidate brief | 2 hours


 The task
 Build a small web app that helps residents find local parks. A resident should be able to see parks on a map,
 browse a list, and open details for a park. Choose a real or fictional municipality.

 Save the full, unredacted AI transcript from every tool you use for this exercise, starting with your first
 prompt. You must submit these logs with your code.

 Spend 90 minutes to 2 hours on the whole submission, including testing and your README. Stop at two
 hours and tell us what you left unfinished. We want a small, polished working app and clear decisions. Extra
 features are not required.

 What to build
 â€¢ A map of the parks. Show where parks are located. Selecting a park should open its details or clearly link
    to them. The app must work without access to the resident's location.
 â€¢ A list of parks. Residents should also be able to find and select parks without using the map.
 â€¢ Park details. Show the available information, such as the name, address, description, amenities, hours, and
    images. Handle missing information without crashing or inventing details.
 â€¢ An accessible interface. Make the main tasks work on a phone and desktop. Use readable text and clear
    labels. Residents should be able to select a park from the list and open its details using a keyboard, with a
    visible focus indicator. The list and details should provide an alternative to interacting with map markers.
 Search, filters, and current-location support are optional. Include them only if the core experience works
 and you have time. A backend, accounts, and a hosted deployment are not required.




                                                                                                               1/3
 Granicus Lighthouse / TECHNICAL INTERVIEWS




 Data and tools
 Use the supplied assets/parks.sample.json. You may extend it or use another public dataset; describe any
 changes in your README. The sample includes missing or empty values. Placeholder images are fine.

 assets/parks.sample.json contains an array of park objects. Each object has this shape:

 {
     "id": "prospect-park",
     "name": "Prospect Park",
     "description": "A 526-acre park in the heart of Brooklyn...",
     "location": {
        "lat": 40.6602,
        "lng": -73.9690,
        "address": "Brooklyn, NY 11225"
     },
     "amenities": ["playground", "dog-run", "trails", "restrooms", "parking"],
     "hours": "6:00 AM - 1:00 AM",
     "images": ["https://example.com/prospect-1.jpg"],
     "acreage": 526,
     "rating": 4.7
 }

 Fields may be missing or null, and arrays may be empty. Handle those cases gracefully. You may extend the
 schema; describe any changes in your README. The image URL above is a placeholder.

 Choose your own language, framework, and map library. Include any setup needed to run the app. Do not
 submit private credentials. If a service requires a key, explain how the interviewer can supply it.

 Use AI coding tools as you normally would. Using AI is expected. You are responsible for understanding and
 checking the submitted code, including code generated by a tool.

 Submit the full, unredacted AI conversation logs, including your prompts and the tool's responses. Do not
 edit, shorten, or select excerpts. If your tool cannot export a conversation, contact the recruiter about an
 alternative.




                                                                                                                2/3
 Granicus Lighthouse / TECHNICAL INTERVIEWS




 What to submit
 Send a zip file containing:

 1. Source code for the app.
 2. A README with run instructions, what works, what you left out, important decisions, known issues, and
    how you checked the result. Include your approximate time spent and the most important next steps
    before public use.
 3. Unredacted AI conversation logs from every tool you used for this exercise.

 Follow-up chat
 We will spend 30 minutes reviewing your submission together. Have the app and code ready to share. You
 do not need slides or additional features.

 Come prepared to:

 â€¢ Demo the app and walk through the code.
 â€¢ Explain your decisions, trade-offs, and what you left out.
 â€¢ Discuss how you used AI, reviewed its output, and checked the app.
 â€¢ Explain what you would change before release, including deployment, maintenance, and likely failures.
 â€¢ Ask questions about the team and role.
 Be ready to show a specific piece of code you reviewed closely and explain how you checked it. If you found
 a mistake, tell us how you found and corrected it. If you did not find one, explain what you checked and what
 you are still unsure about.

 How we evaluate
 1. Usefulness for residents. Can someone find a park and view its details? Is the app accessible and usable?
    Did you prioritize the main tasks?
 2. Communication. Can you explain what you chose, why you chose it, and what you left out in terms your
    audience can understand?
 3. Code quality and maintainability. Is the code readable and straightforward to extend? Does it handle
    missing data and failures sensibly?
 4. AI direction and accountability. Did you guide the tools, check their output, and take responsibility for
    the result?
 5. Review and verification. Can you show how you reviewed the code and checked its behavior, including
    problems that passing tests might miss?
 A modest app that works and is well explained is more useful than an ambitious app with broken core
 features.

 You are not expected to solve every production concern in two hours. Make reasonable assumptions where
 the prompt is silent and record them in your README. Contact the recruiter if a missing file or setup
 problem prevents you from starting.

item.text:
Implemented park details on `feature/details`. All four required checks passed.

| Command | Result |
|---|---|
| `npm run typecheck` | Passed |
| `npm run lint` | Passed |
| `npm test` | 31 tests passed across 4 files |
| `npm run build` | Production build succeeded |

**Files changed** under `src/components/ParkDetails/` only. Updated [ParkDetails.tsx](./src/components/ParkDetails/ParkDetails.tsx) and added [ParkDetails.css](./src/components/ParkDetails/ParkDetails.css), [formatAmenity.ts](./src/components/ParkDetails/formatAmenity.ts), [ParkDetails.test.tsx](./src/components/ParkDetails/ParkDetails.test.tsx), and [formatAmenity.test.ts](./src/components/ParkDetails/formatAmenity.test.ts). `App.tsx`, `App.test.tsx`, and `src/styles.css` were untouched. No dependencies, commits, or pushes.

**Behavior verified**

- Selecting a park focuses its name heading. The initial empty state leaves focus alone, and re-rendering the same park preserves the user’s current focus.
- Missing address or hours display “Not provided.” Other missing facts are omitted. Tests cover literal `null` and `undefined` leaks, `0 acres`, `1 acre`, and `0 out of 5`.
- Each photo loads lazily with park-specific alt text. A load error replaces only that image with an “Image unavailable” block, so there is no fallback request loop. Parks with no photos omit the gallery.

**Integration check:** “Back to list” calls `onClose`. After the branches are combined, verify that App/list restores keyboard focus to the previously selected list item.
